cards.title: Core foundations: each member has one meaning, a Jet body or a typed provider leaf, with no duplicate dispatcher row
cards.body:
Destination: each foundational Core member (text, collections, math, units, time, encoding, regex, args, files and path, io and mem, portable crypto) has exactly one meaning: its Jet body in Core, or a declared typed provider leaf. No dispatcher row or tier-specific route duplicates it, and every caller and generated projection uses that one contract.

Why it matters: two meanings for one member is an I9 risk (tiers disagree) and keeps the Rust-era routing alive.

State: Compiler/Prelude/Core.rows lists the source_module ownership and the remaining dispatcher rows; Tools/agent/CoreSurfaceLedger.jet checks the surface.

Other items that were here moved to focused cards on 2026-11-15: names, modules and prelude to the Core names card, I/O failures to the Core I/O failures card, and single items to #6314, #6877, #3549, #4524, #6367, #6873 and #3836.
cards.plan:
**Goal.** This is the foundations wave of #3690 (W1 plus part of W2). Each foundational Core member (text, collections, math, units, time, encoding, regex, args, files/path, io/mem, portable crypto) gets exactly one meaning: its Jet body in Core/*.jet, or a declared typed provider leaf. No Rust dispatcher row, JIT shim or interpreter route may duplicate it.

**Current state.**
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.jet` (2412 lines) holds 1,814 `dispatcher_row`s. 693 are in foundation modules, and 657 of those name members the module's `source_module … owns {…}` line already gives to Jet. Those are duplicate meanings and an I9 risk.

| Module | Rows | Jet-owned |
|---|---|---|
| math | 220 | 219 |
| text | 137 | 137 |
| encoding | 124 | 123 |
| collections | 52 | 52 |
| time | 48 | 39 |
| files | 45 | 38 |
| crypto | 42 | 25 |
| regex | 20 | 19 |
| args | 3 | 3 |
| mem | 2 | 2 |

- The remaining 36 unowned rows (crypto 17, time 9, files 7, math/encoding/regex 1 each) need either a Jet body or a leaf declaration.
- The self-hosted routing mirror is `Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/{CoreCallRows,CoreCalls,CoreHostSignatures}.jet`, `Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Codegen/HandleMethods.jet` and `Compiler/JetEval/Source/Routes/`.
- From merged #3517: the text/file source attempts were reverted on 2026-09-21 because the compiler rejected private source paths. `Core/text/string.jet` is now a private source part (`crates/jet-foundation/src/CoreSourceParts.rs:30`).
- c4 is met, but #3584 (building) now requires ALL_CAPS module constants. c7 tracks that.

cards.title: System Core modules are fully Jet-owned: every declaration has a Jet body or a policy-free provider leaf, with typed failures
cards.body:
Destination: the system Core modules (archive, net, service, sys, log, http, term, sync, db, event, process, tasks, watcher, email) are ordinary Jet. Every declaration has a Jet body or a typed, policy-free provider leaf; protocol, policy, validation and typed failures live in Jet source; and failure and effect proofs pass on O0, O1 and O2.

Why it matters: Core is ordinary Jet that uses only mechanisms any package can use (philosophy pillar 5), and the same program means the same on every tier (I9).

cards.title: Jetpack in Jet: port the package and environment engine from Rust to Jet
cards.body:
OWNER DIRECTIVE 2026-09-27 (lifts the 2026-08-30 Jetpack-in-Jet pause recorded on #2327): the owner authorizes a full port of Jetpack from Rust to Jet. The compiler port under Compiler/ (#218) runs in parallel as a sibling; follow its conventions. Phases in order: (1) complete code build-out, (2) parity and bug fixing, (3) optimization.

Owner instructions (override default routing in AGENTS.md for this stream):
- Opus 5.5 only: every dispatched subagent runs on Opus 5.5, set explicitly on OMP task/hub. No @implementation, @full_review, @cavecrew, or other default profile/model. If a dispatch cannot run on Opus 5.5, stop that slice and report; never fall back.
- No JetOS work: do not port, stub, test, benchmark or plan crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/, crates/jetos, or any command/provider/image path that exists only for JetOS. Omit JetOS hooks from ported code; exclude JetOS surfaces from the parity harness and performance cells.
- All ported code lives under top-level Jetpack/, laid out as Jetpack/<Area>/Source/... mirroring Compiler/, plus Jetpack/Bootstrap/ with an ordered sources.list and check script modeled on Compiler/Bootstrap.
- Scope (non-test LOC, ~117k, JetOS excluded): crates/jetpack (~100k incl. src/bin helpers), crates/jetpack-bin (~0.2k), crates/jet-nix-eval (~3.8k), crates/jet-store (~3.2k), crates/jet-env-model (~11k), crates/jet-pkg-model (~69k). jet-env-model and jet-pkg-model are shared with the compiler: check Compiler/ ownership first and never create a second copy. Use Compiler/ Jet versions of jet-driver, jet-sema, jet-codegen, etc., not new ports.
- Every Rust module except JetOS maps to a named Jet home; the mapping and progress live in Tower cards only, not docs.
- Phase 1 order: models + Nix evaluator; Store (Nar, Archive, Journal, Cache, Lifecycle, Closure, ...); Trust, TrustRoot, SemanticLock; Provider, ProviderGraph; Services, Shell, Image (OCI only), Recipe; CLI. Idiomatic current Jet, not transliterated Rust (audits list anti-patterns). Port unit/integration tests with each module. Each slice passes the Jetpack bootstrap check and runs on AOT and default jet run (I9).
- Compiler defects/missing Core APIs: file or reuse a Tower card; no workaround inside Jetpack. New syntax/public API/dependencies need an owner ballot. ed25519-dalek and zstd need an approved bridge pattern (I6); no new external deps. No #Unsafe without an audited reason.
- Phase 2: differential harness running Rust jetpack and the Jet build on the same inputs (existing tests such as tests/jetpack_platform, fixtures, real projects), comparing stdout, stderr, exit codes, store contents and lockfiles; drive every difference to zero with root fixes. Rust Jetpack stays shipped until an owner cutover decision.
- Phase 3: strict gate vs Rust Jetpack, Jet/Rust <= 1.05 on every cell: warm jetpack env, store verification, hashing, graph load; record in the canonical manifest. Never trade semantics for speed.
- Operating: Tower only ledger; one writer per path; worktrees only under .agent-worktrees/; commands via scripts/agent/jet-env; scratch in ~/.cache/jet-luna; narrow proofs per card, broad suites at milestones; report exercised receipts.

Done: every non-JetOS Rust module has a ported Jet home under Jetpack/ with tests, the parity harness passes, every performance cell meets the gate; then stop and ask the owner for the cutover decision.
cards.plan:
## Goal
This is the epic for the owner-authorized (2026-09-27) port of Jetpack from Rust to Jet under top-level `Jetpack/`. It runs in three phases: (1) code build-out, (2) parity and bug fixing, (3) optimization. The Rust Jetpack stays the shipped implementation until the owner ratifies a cutover ballot.

## Owner rules (preserved)
- Every dispatched subagent runs Opus 5.5, set explicitly; never fall back.
- No JetOS work of any kind.
- Code lives in `Jetpack/<Area>/Source/…` with `Jetpack/Bootstrap/` (ordered `sources.list`/`tests.list`, `check.sh`).
- The mapping and progress live only in Tower cards.
- Reuse Compiler/ and never create a second copy.
- Compiler defects and Core gaps get Tower cards and no workaround.
- New syntax, public API or dependencies need an owner ballot. ed25519/zstd need an approved bridge (I6).
- No `#Unsafe` without an audited reason.
- Write idiomatic current Jet and port the tests with each module.

## Current state
- About 96k Jet lines across 12 of 13 areas (tracked plus in-flight). Foundation 2.8k, PackageModel 38.9k (32 test files), EnvModel 8.4k, NixEval 5.6k, Nix 2.4k, Store 25.0k (15), Trust 4.5k, Recipe 0.5k, Provider 4.9k (3), Environment 0.4k, Image 0.8k, CLI 2.1k. Services is empty. The area DAG is `Jetpack/Bootstrap/areas.list:9-23`.
- Much of PackageModel/Store/EnvModel is untracked working-tree work after the rate-limit stop (963c3cb09); the slices (#3601-#3615, #3637-#3652, …) own it.
- No differential harness and no Jetpack performance cells exist yet.
- `check.sh` supports `--syntax`, `--area X [--deps-from-head]`, `--each` and `--tests`. It prints `JETPACK CHECK OK (check, default run, AOT test)` and a receipt with `check-unit-sha256`.

## Changes (in order)
1. Build-out (criterion 1): finish every slice card. Each one ends with `check.sh --area <Area> --deps-from-head --tests` green and a receipt.
2. Integrated proof (criterion 2): `check.sh --each --tests` and then a whole-unit `check.sh --tests` on main. Run a `#Unsafe` audit by searching `Jetpack/` for `#Unsafe` and checking every hit for a reason.
3. Parity (criterion 3): a differential harness under `Jetpack/Bootstrap/` that runs Rust `jetpack` and the Jet build on the root `tests/jetpack_*.rs` inputs, fixtures and real projects (JetOS excluded), and diffs stdout, stderr, exit code, store tree and lockfiles.
4. Performance (criterion 4): warm `jetpack env`, store verification, hashing and graph-load cells in the canonical performance manifest, strict gate Jet/Rust ≤ 1.05.
5. Stop point (criterion 5): raise the owner cutover ballot.

## Proof
- `Tools/agent/jet-env bash Jetpack/Bootstrap/check.sh --each --tests` → every area prints `JETPACK CHECK OK (check, default run, AOT test)`.
- `Tools/agent/jet-env bash Jetpack/Bootstrap/check.sh --tests` → `JETPACK CHECK OK (check, default run, AOT test)`. Record the receipt and unit SHA.
- The differential harness report shows 0 differences. The perf gate shows every Jetpack cell ≤ 1.05.

## Batch
batch-jetpack-cli: CLI is the top of the area DAG, so its unit closes over every area. The epic's integrated proof is that unit.

## Dependencies
- #3661: the single-unit `jet check` is too slow, so the whole-unit check times out or hits the memory cap.
- #3673: cross-module enums, type imports and constants, needed to split areas into packages.
- #3676: the first ICE of the tier run.
- The Core gap cards #3593-#3598 and the Compiler entry points #3599 stay on the slices that need them.

cards.title: Project jobs run the same on every tier: `jet <job>` and `jet jobs` dispatch, typed arguments, `after:` order, validation, freshness and inspection
cards.body:
Destination: a #Job declared once runs by name (`jet <job>`, `jet jobs <job>`, `jet run -- <job>`) with typed scalar parameters from argv, its `after:` predecessors in order, validation before any effect, declared input/output freshness, and one process and job identity model for inspection and lifecycle events, with byte-identical output from a built binary and from `jet jobs`.

Why: project commands are how users drive their work; a job that behaves differently on another tier breaks trust.

History: the 2026-09-28 owner-reported defects (core.process compile, ignored `after:`, E1321 on parameter jobs) were fixed in the retired Rust compiler and met as c1-c3. Today the Jet driver does not make parameter jobs argv-selectable (Pipeline.jet:2685-2688) and the top-level `jet <job>` lookup is unbuilt (Front.jet:1688-1717 against Docs/spec cli.md). Source generation through #Job is #6952.
cards.plan: Build argv selection for parameter jobs and the top-level `jet <job>` lookup in the Jet driver, then turn the jetpack_tasks rows green. Each criterion names its case.

cards.title: Diagnostic readability sweep: rewrite every active diagnostic in plain words (Opus 5.5 workers)
cards.body:
Destination: every active diagnostic reads in plain words, enforced so it cannot regress:
- What names the learner's specific problem, using the names in their code.
- Why gives the reason in one or two plain sentences.
- Fix gives a concrete edit or command.
- No internal vocabulary: decision IDs, constant names, 'unit', byte offsets, stage names. That material lives in `jet explain CODE --verbose` and `--json`.

Why it matters: owner-directed P0 (2026-09-28, learnability report F17). A census of 813 active rows found 218 with a placeholder Why, 297 whose What repeats the internal meaning, and 287 with decision IDs in user-facing text. The research basis is Becker et al. 2019, Barik et al. 2018 and Ko et al. 2004.

The authority is the diagnostic registry; Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet is generated from it.

Related cards (2026-11-15 split): stop locations and traces #6915, error values in handlers #6916, progress output #6917, user-visible text case #6734, IOError #6881, ComputeError #6624.
cards.plan:
## Goal
Owner-directed P0 (2026-09-28, learnability report F17). Every active diagnostic reads in plain words:
- **What** names the learner's specific problem, using the names in their code.
- **Why** gives the reason in one or two plain sentences, with no placeholder.
- **Fix** gives a concrete edit or command.
- No internal vocabulary: decision IDs, constant names, "unit", "source bytes", byte offsets, key=value dumps, stage names. That material moves to `jet explain CODE --verbose` and `--json`.

The rubric is enforced so the sweep cannot regress.

## Current state
- The authority is `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Diagnostics.jet`. `Compiler/Bootstrap/generate-diagnostic-rows.mjs:9-10` generates `Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet` from it.
- The 2026-09-28 census found 813 active rows: 218 with the placeholder Why "The registered <stage> rule applies here" (for example `Diagnostics.jet:7-8`, E0001/E0002), 297 whose What repeats Meaning, and 287 with decision IDs in human text.
- E0114 (probe p08) still says "its final statement produces no value … statements and semicolon-terminated expressions yield unit" (`tests/ui/missing_return.stderr`, `tests/ui/total_guard_missing_value.stderr`). It is produced only in Rust (`crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Registration.rs:969`, `CheckerCore/blocks.rs:199`); JetSema has no E0114.
- `tests/diagnostics_format.rs` already checks row completeness and sentence case (`:13-75`), but not placeholder text or decision IDs.
- Rows owned by other open P0 cards are sequenced first: #3715 (E0121), #3718 (authority errors) and #3719 (unclosed delimiter).

## Changes
1. **Docs.** Write the rubric into `Docs/spec/diagnostics.md`.
2. **Validator.** Add `every_active_diagnostic_reads_in_plain_words` to `tests/diagnostics_format.rs`, and apply the same checks in `generate-diagnostic-rows.mjs` so generation fails on a violation.
3. **Rewrite.** Rewrite the rows in `Diagnostics.jet` using disjoint code-range lanes run by `opus-worker` (Claude Opus 5.5), with one integration owner. Update the dynamic message builders in `crates/jet-parser` and `crates/jet-sema` that fill those rows, then regenerate `DiagnosticRows.jet`.
4. **E0114.** Add E0114 to JetSema (the final-statement check in the block/return analysis) and have it name the uncovered path's condition. Mirror the path-naming in `crates/jet-sema/.../blocks.rs` for the shipped binary.
5. **Snapshots.** Re-bless every affected UI snapshot one fixture at a time (`JET_UI_FILTER=<f> UPDATE_EXPECT=<f>`, with `UPDATE_EXPECT_REASON`). The orchestrator reviews each change as text.
6. **Probes.** Re-run the report's Appendix A probes on a fresh build. A probe that no longer reproduces is recorded on the card.

## Proof
- `cargo test --test diagnostics_format`: all tests pass, including the new rubric test, which is the census. Log its counts on the card.
- `cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots ui_snapshots` and `cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots lint_snapshots`: pass after reviewed re-blessing.
- `JET_UI_FILTER=tests/ui/missing_return.jet cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots ui_snapshots`: pass.
- `Tools/agent/jet-env bash Compiler/Bootstrap/check.sh`: exit 0.
- Every lane returns `Tools/agent/lane-check.sh` `CHECK OK`, and the lanes are listed on the card.

## Batch
`batch-jetc-sema`: diagnostic registry text and sema message builders, proven by the UI/format suites in one retest pass.

## Dependencies
#3715, #3718 and #3719 (all P0, ready) own overlapping rows and land first.

cards.title: Binary encoding: bounded sign_extend and exact max_bytes accounting (D-BINARY-CANONICAL1)
cards.body:
Implement the single checked pack and unpack contract in core.encoding.binary, as ratified in D-BINARY-CANONICAL1. Errors use the source BinaryError form. Acceptance: pack then unpack is the identity on every fixed-width type, and invalid widths are rejected.

Earlier text, kept for reference (Rust-era homes such as Rust crates, TIR/MIR/LIR, the JIT and generated Rust are retired):

Found 2026-10-03 by the runtime port (RtW11-BINARY-CRC, probe ~/.cache/jet-test-scratch/RtW11-BINARY-CRC/RUNTIME-BINARY-CRC-1/probe/unit.jet). Today the Jet source Core and the native (frozen Rust EncodingBase.rs:239-520) tiers give different meanings for the same program (I9 split):
- pack_u8(300): source returns Err(BinaryError.Range); native wraps to [44].
- pack with "@H": source Err(Format); native treats @/= as little-endian, giving [1,0].
- fixed pack: native infallible; source signatures are BinaryError! (E2402 at callers).
- generic errors: native String mapped to canonical Err.message; source typed BinaryError.
- unpack: native accepts trailing bytes; source does not. u64 to I64: native preserves bits.
Options (same programs distinguish them: overflow 300, "@H", trailing bytes, sign bits):
A. Adopt the frozen native policy as canonical: fixed I64 wrapping, infallible fixed packs, generic APIs Err!, trailing bytes accepted; migrate public source callers/errors; settle whether exact-Int arguments narrow.
B. Keep the checked source behavior (typed BinaryError, range and format errors, no trailing bytes) as canonical and repair the native/JIT consumers to match.
Recommendation: B (checked by default per philosophy; wrapping hides data loss). Until ruled, the port keeps its kernel private and changes no public behavior.

cards.title: Scripting measured against every peer: the ScriptBench gate, the run phases and the peer audit
cards.body:
Owner ruling, 2026-10-28. This replaces the old rule where a `#!` first line silently granted every permission.

In plain words: a Jet script gets no extra powers just by having a `#!` line. The first time it needs one (reading files, the network, and so on), Jet asks you in the terminal, once. Your answer is remembered for that exact script. If you already wrote `-A` (allow all), Jet does not ask. Printing, arguments, stdin, time, randomness and exit are always free.

Behavior:
1. A `#!` launch line no longer grants anything implicitly (today `jet_cli_source_invocation` in Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/Authority.jet sets `all = true` for any `#!/` file).
2. `-A` (or `--allow=...`) written on the launch line, e.g. `#!/usr/bin/env -S jet -A`, applies as if typed. `./script` and `jet run script.jet` behave the same. `-A` on the command line works as today.
3. Ask once: when the run needs a permission it was not given and stdin/stderr are a terminal, Jet asks before the program starts. Sema already knows the required effects, so one prompt lists every missing permission and its resource, for example "read files under ./data" or "connect to the network". It offers allow once, always allow this script, and no. "Always" is remembered against the script's content hash in the project's single top-level `.jet/` (or the user cache for loose scripts). If the content changes, Jet asks again.
4. With -A present, Jet never asks. Outside a terminal (CI, pipes), Jet never asks either: it fails with the exact-grant error (5).
5. Exact-grant errors name the smallest grant (e.g. `--allow=FS.Read:./data`) and also say that `-A` grants every effect. `jet fix` writes the chosen grant onto the launch line (scripts) or into package.jet (packages).
6. Free basics: stdout/stderr printing, args, stdin, env-free time reads, randomness and exit never need a grant.
7. `--verbose` under -A prints one line listing the effects the run actually used, so users learn what to narrow.

One meaning on every tier (I9): the prompt and grants live in the shared CLI authority path, not per backend.

cards.title: Cache control and visibility: give programs control over L1/L2/L3 use and show where code leaves cache for RAM or disk
cards.body:
Owner question 2026-10-30 (verbatim): 'Cache hits are critical -> how can we give control over L1,2,3 cache, visualize when we are no longer in cache & go to RAM or HDD/SSD?'

cards.body:

cards.title: Binary size: Jet's default build must produce the smallest output of any language, for every program, by design rather than per-program tricks
cards.body: Owner (2026-10-30): 437 KB for hello world is far too big. Measured by Main on this machine (x86-64 Linux, $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/hello): Zig 0.15.2 ReleaseSmall 10,720 B (static), Zig ReleaseFast stripped 18,744 B, C gcc -O2 stripped 14,440 B (dynamic glibc), C musl static stripped 17,696 B, Rust 1.97.1 -O stripped 394,032 B (dynamic). Jet with #6106 C1 (per-function sections plus gc): 437,416 B with .text 387,880 B (IrTypes-2 measurement); dev before #6106 C1: 5,210,576 B. A hand-written static ELF hello is a few hundred bytes. The size comes from runtime code that startup and print reach (allocator, task and thread setup, panic and formatting machinery), not from the program.

Owner asked (2026-11-15) whether precompiled Core should serve only jet run, not jet build. Main's answer (operational), recorded here:
- Shipped Core machine code is already run-only. jet run binds its Core calls to the shipped code. jet build binds none (case a_run_binds_its_core_calls_to_the_shipped_core_code: core_calls 0 on build) and compiles the Core it calls together with the program, so O2 keeps cross-module inlining, specialization and dead-code removal. That stays.
- Checked Core (no re-checking of Core source) should serve both. Checking means the same thing at every level, build time is a required cell under the 30M lines/s cold target, and a run-only checked form would leave two Core front ends (I8) with jet build never gaining.
- The one place build loses today, A2a's double parse of mostly reached modules (#6759 log), is being fixed at its root rather than routed around.
If the owner wants run-only checking anyway, it becomes option F on D-PRECORE-SPEED1.

Main ruling H12 (fact): rendering a reported diagnostic's span from embedded Core text is display, not reading Core source; it may happen only when a diagnostic is reported, so a clean compile reads 0 bytes of Core text. H16 (a B step that slows a 6.2 program vs c37 never-slower) is owner-only: PrecompiledCore-4 drafts the ballot; until it is ratified, no B step that slows a program merges.

The cause is the runtime, which links 76 KB of code and 11 KB of unwind tables into every program, used or not: jet_rt core 17.2 KB, allocator 13.2, production receipt 6.5, trap and fault report 5.7, helpers 5.0, scheduler 4.5, host 4.3, sync/vDSO 3.5, plus threads, sentry and comptime-stop. Features that every program genuinely needs (fault report, trap) stay, minimized and never drop — Criterion: The runtime links by reach: a hello program links no scheduler, threads, sentry or production-receipt code, and every runtime part it does link is called on its path. Proof: `nm --size-sort` of the batch-jet hello build lists no jet_rt scheduler, thread, sentry or receipt symbols, and a second program that spawns a task does link the scheduler and prints the same output on o0, o1 and o2.

questions.text: the real issue here doesnt seem to me to be the fact that jet has a crash report or even that it is included, but the fact that it is so freaking massive. we need to find ways to shrink it by orders of magnitude
questions.answer: You're right: the problem was the report's size, not its presence. It adds 29,730 bytes to hello (measured on dev 94e290bb4a). Finding a function and its line takes 10,554 of that: a section-header walk, mapping the program file, the load bias and the table decode. The report bodies and frame walk take 10,457, the source snippet 5,543, the writers 1,656, the alternate-stack setup 523, and text and data 997. Most of it comes from the runtime's unoptimized code generation. Each comparison is computed twice, each function saves five registers, and each checked add carries a 40-byte stop call, which also links the program-stop path, allocator and scheduler. Once the program owns its entry, those stay in hello only because of the report, and the size model then keeps hello at 79,281 bytes. We rebuilt the report as a 2,197-byte machine-code prototype (c6328/report/report.S): 1,712 bytes of code, 485 of message text and 32 of data. It prints the same text from the same table format. Two link symbols find the table, one stack buffer replaces the allocator and formatter, and it walks frame pointers instead of using an unwinder. All 16 parity cases match, including the E3012 golden byte for byte. A program whose stack bound is proven cannot overflow, so it can drop the E3012 branch and come down to 1,444 bytes with the same output. With every planned step, hello is 2,599 bytes, against 504 with the one-line note. Nothing users see changes, except that `strip` now keeps the 67-byte location table. We therefore recommend withdrawing the ballot. The rewritten JSON, which recommends keeping the full report everywhere at its new size, is there if you want it on record.

questions.text: still sounds very large, work backwards from optimized hand written asm or binary and anything that puts us above it must be justified. if you have a VERY good legitimate reason, (e.g. in a program that uses runtime feature x, there is y amount of byte overhead to support that feature, but otherwise all machine code has been perfectly optimized by codegen so there is no bloat, bulk, or fluff.)
questions.answer:
We started from hand-written hello: 253 bytes. The release report now prints the signal line, the build id and the frame addresses, then re-raises the signal. It is 840 bytes of measured assembly, so release hello is 1,185 bytes, 932 above the floor.

Names, lines, source snippets and the Why/Fix text moved out of the program into `jet crash`, which reads the side file by build id. That removed 1,357 bytes plus the table (67 B in hello, 91,771 B in the release HTTP server). Dev builds (`jet run`, `jet test`, `jet dev`) keep today's full text.

Everything else is paid only by programs that use the feature:
- stack overflow: 200 B plus one word
- threads: 27 B plus a word
- Secret: 27 B plus a word
- buffered stdout: 14 B plus a word
- the first writable word adds a 56 B segment header

The budget table is in the ballot.

questions.text: what the fuck wouldnt this massively inflate deliverable binary sizes???
questions.answer: Yes, it did. 662 KB (21%) of the 3.12 MB release HTTP server was debug info the running program never reads: 338 KB of DWARF, 232 KB of symbol table and 92 KB of crash table. The ballot now recommends shipping none of it. The release binary holds only code and data plus a 92-byte build id: 2.46 MB. The debug info goes to a side file that Jet files in a local symbol store under that id. jet run and jet crash print the full crash report with names and lines from it, and jet debug (or gdb through debuginfod) attaches with the side file. Measurements and design: ballot D-RELEASE-DEBUG1.

cards.title: Run time: default codegen must be borderline equal to hand-written optimized assembly for every program
cards.body: Owner order, 2026-10-30: performance should be borderline equal to hand-written assembly with default codegen, not with flags or per-program tricks. Binary size has the same goal, and #6328 owns size. This card owns speed. Every program in the perf corpus (one per required perf cell plus the codegen kernels: loops, bounds-checked indexing, string length and iteration, slices, calls, closures, records, allocation, I/O write) gets a hand-written, optimized x86-64 assembly reference, committed with a harness that measures cycles and instructions (perf stat, best of N, pinned CPU). The gap is closed in the code generator and runtime design (instruction selection, register allocation, bounds-check elimination, inlining, layout), never by weakening safety, semantics or diagnostics (AGENTS.md performance gate).

Evidence from G1Lead (#6688 c4, 7639370892 and b53d287e41; Jet libm against musl with identical bits, O1 perf-stat cycles per call: sin 81.8 vs 64.8, cos 80.5 vs 64.7, exp 56.7 vs 39.9, log 63.4 vs 41.1, pow 169.3 vs 113.9). Roots, all general codegen: (1) index math on a proven-small Int keeps an inline add plus jo overflow test, 2 to 3 per access; a comptime table read goes through its static list header (len and data-pointer loads) with a bounds check and a list_bounds_stop call with xmm spills, about 15 instructions per access (exp 2, log 4, pow 5 accesses). (2) FloatBits and FloatFromBits (BuildLibrary ir_reinterpret) and Float abs (BuildRoutes:3489) go through a stack store and reload instead of movq; 14 percent of pow samples sit on one reload. (3) At O1, Float and shifted constants are neither folded nor hoisted: movabs plus movq at every use. (4) A || chain is materialized as bools through stack slots, about 25 instructions at pow entry. (5) A small struct return (LibmReduced) goes through sret, and a small helper (libm_rem_pio2_near) is not inlined. Same family as the TlsLead hash findings above; ownership is owner Q17.

Evidence from TlsLead (#6694 S1, b53a78981d), the emitted x64 of core_crypto___jet_hashes_dcompress (portable SHA-512 compress, about 935 ns per block against about 280 ns for mbedtls): (1) 4670 instructions, 2564 mov and 1209 rbp spills, about 6 GPRs used (#6478); (2) no rol or ror: a constant rotate lowers to a shift-by-cl pair plus and 0x1f, and there are 107 shl or shr 0x20 U32 zero-extends; (3) per call 65 jet_rt_list_bounds_stop, 76 jet_ir_stop_poll inside fixed-trip loops (#6472), 32 cleanup enter and leave, 43 jet_rt_int_drop; (4) wrapping(U8{x}) from an out-of-range Int costs about 260 ns (global masks, boxed-Int drops, jo checks) against 9 ns for U8{x %% 256}; (5) list copy and push cost 1.5 to 2 ns per element; (6) a fixed-list global is re-materialized on every access (64 stores); (7) hash_start plus Close costs about 256 ns. Each is a general codegen root; the crypto engine is the second program for the perf rule.

criteria.text: Work backwards from hand-optimized machine code (owner direction 2026-11-11). A kernel catalog covers each common code shape: counted and iterator loops, list sum and map, text scan and compare, struct copy and move, enum match, option and error return, hash lookup, bounds-checked index, call and return, allocation and drop. Each kernel has a small Jet program and a hand-written, maximally optimized x86-64 reference that does the same work with the same safety checks. For each kernel, a checker compares the hot code that `jet build` emits with the reference: instruction count, spills, loads and stores, checks, and calls. Every extra instruction is named with its root (bounds check not hoisted, value spilled, copy not elided, loop not vectorized, call not inlined, or atomic reference count). Each root is fixed once, in the general lowering, never per kernel, and is proved on a second program that uses the feature differently. Each kernel then gets a machine-code golden that pins the emitted hot loop at O1 and O2, so a regression fails the gate. The gate fails any kernel whose emitted hot code is over its reference in instructions or cycles. Every new codegen feature adds its kernel and reference before it lands. Proof: `node Tools/perf/asm-parity/asm-parity.mjs --jet $JET --gate` over the catalog cells and `jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter codegen_kernels` (machine-code goldens at O1 and O2), with instructions per element recorded before and after each step.

cards.title: Require one typed hole in dispatch tables and preserve Boolean guards
cards.body:
User proposed factoring the repeated condition in examples/features/basics/fizzbuzz.jet into an if header with one required `_` hole. He chose one statically typed input, ordinary && and || composition, and header evaluation per attempted arm. This card records the complete language choice before implementation.

The proposal preserves candidate guards, pattern bindings, range matching, and the existing ordinary and subjectless if forms. It replaces old distributed headers in one repository-wide cutover. The full ballot must settle exact typing, grouping, evaluation, ownership, exhaustiveness, and migration rules. These rules are not implemented or ratified by creating this card.

Deduplication: the live non-done card query found no matching typed-hole, hole-dispatch, FizzBuzz, or D-IFDIST1 stream. D-IFHOLE1 is unused. This request is about readability, not a claimed performance improvement.
cards.plan:
## Goal
Implement ratified D-IFHOLE1=A (2026-09-11). Every dispatch table header holds exactly one statically typed `_` hole that each non-else arm fills. Guards keep ordinary `&&`/`||`.

```jet
fn label(n: Int) -> String {
    return if n % _ == 0 {
        15 -> "FizzBuzz"
        3 -> "Fizz"
        5 -> "Buzz"
        else -> "{n}"
    }
}
```

## Ratified terms (keep all)
- `2 && ready` needs both checks. `2 && ready || emergency` accepts emergency alone. `2 && (ready || emergency)` always tests the candidate.
- Boolean candidates are grouped in parentheses. Arm-level `|` separates candidates, not bits.
- Value tables normally need `else`. Omitting `else` requires plain equality, one immutable bound subject and complete unguarded pattern coverage.
- Owner choices: one candidate per non-else arm; a candidate behind a false `&&` is left uncalled; the header is evaluated once per attempted arm (bind first for a single read).
- Amends D-IFDIST1, D-IF3, D-MATCHARM1/2 and S68, and preserves D-ARMHEAD-PAREN1.

## Current state
- `Examples/features/basics/fizzbuzz.jet:5-11` uses a subjectless table. The hole form sits commented out at `:14-21`, in retired `String ->` spelling.
- The distributed header `if subject OP { atoms -> }` is parsed by `parser_expression_form_parse_dispatch_table` in `Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/ExpressionForms/DecisionTables.jet:340`. It lowers to nested ifs through `parser_expression_form_nest_arms` (`:284`), with atom/`&&`/`||` handling at `:135-213` and E0386 at `:188`. There is no hole parsing anywhere in JetParser.
- D-IFHOLE1 is not recorded in syntax-decisions.md or Syntax.rs.
- Migration size: about 6,050 tracked `.jet` lines open an `if <expr> OP {` table, most of them `if x == {` pattern tables. The migration must be mechanical.

## Changes
1. JetParser DecisionTables.jet: parse `if H[_] { candidate [&& guard] -> body }`. Reject a missing, repeated or ambiguous hole with registered errors. A holeless distributed header is not Jet syntax: it gets an ordinary parse error, with no teaching diagnostic or Safe edit (owner order). No compatibility parse path.
2. JetAst: carry the hole position, or desugar at parse time by substituting each candidate into the header, so each candidate is evaluated at its substituted position at most once.
3. JetSema (`Expressions/Control.jet`, `Patterns.jet`):
   - a single hole type across arms, and a Bool header result;
   - pattern-slot filling that keeps range matching, payload wildcards and safe bindings;
   - OR groups that cannot leak missing bindings;
   - no exhaustiveness credit unless the subject is immutable.
4. Reuse the existing guard/pattern TIR, so Compiler/JetCodegen needs no new mechanism.
5. Register the new diagnostics in DiagnosticRows.jet and Prelude/Diagnostics.jet, with UI fixtures `tests/ui/ifhole_{missing,repeated,wrong_type,non_bool}.jet`.
6. Apply the Safe edit repo-wide (`jet fix`) across Examples, Core, Compiler, Jetpack, Tools and tests. Bind effectful subjects first where a one-time read was relied on. Update fizzbuzz.jet.
7. Add the syntax registry row and syntax-decisions entry, update the crates/jet-parser formatter, run `jet devtools grammars`, and re-bless snapshots.

## Proof
- `Tools/agent/jet-env bash Compiler/Bootstrap/check.sh` exits 0.
- `JET_GOLDEN_FILTER=basics/fizzbuzz Tools/agent/jet-env cargo test --test golden examples_compile_and_run` passes. The full output, including the countdown, is unchanged on `jet run`, `jet run --interpret` and `jet build`.
- A new `Examples/features/basics/dispatch_hole.jet` golden covers guard precedence, per-attempt header effects (counter), skipped candidates, error propagation and a pattern slot, and matches the explicit reference forms.
- `JET_UI_FILTER=tests/ui/ifhole_ ... cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots ui_snapshots` passes.
- A census of holeless `if <expr> OP {` headers finds zero.

## Batch
batch-jetc-front: parser-led syntax cutover. The sema checks ride the same build.

## Dependencies
None. Land after #3727 so the census and grammar regenerations do not collide.
cards.checkSteps:
All commands run through scripts/agent/jet-env with CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 and disk-backed scratch. These are future proof commands, not completed evidence.

Rebuild with cargo build --bin jet before compiler smoke tests. Run target/debug/jet run --trace-tiers examples/features/basics/fizzbuzz.jet, target/debug/jet run --trace-tiers --interpret examples/features/basics/fizzbuzz.jet, and target/debug/jet run --release examples/features/basics/fizzbuzz.jet. All must retain the complete expected output, including the countdown. The traces must identify default native and forced interpreter execution honestly.

Set JET_GOLDEN_FILTER=basics/fizzbuzz and run cargo test --test golden examples_compile_and_run -- --exact --nocapture. Repeat with the exact path selector for each affected example; never run the unfiltered census for this card.

Migrate and run cargo test --test same_subject_dispatch rewrite_compiles_formats_and_preserves_parser_dispatch_behavior -- --exact --nocapture. Keep its observable original/rewrite execution comparison. Remove source-substring assertions rather than repinning implementation details.

Extend the existing web arm/pattern checks to execute generated JavaScript and Wasm. Use the existing web_build runner and run its exact changed test names with cargo test --test web_build NAME -- --exact --nocapture. The current web_value_and_range_arm_tables_emit_on_js_and_wasm case pins generated text; replace those assertions with observable value/range outcomes. Require real execution, not source-shape evidence or skipped tools.

Use JET_UI_FILTER=tests/ui/NAME.jet with cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots ui_snapshots -- --exact --nocapture for each changed diagnostic fixture. Use the corresponding tests/ui_lint selector and lint_snapshots filter when a generated repair changes. Bless only the exact reviewed fixture, never UPDATE_EXPECT=1.

Add focused regression cases for Boolean precedence, header and candidate effect order, alternative guard failure, missing pattern bindings under OR, ownership after a false guard, and changing-subject exhaustiveness. Their names and exact commands must be recorded before the implementation receipt. Execute the same witness meanings through AOT, default native run, forced interpreter/deopt, web, and compile-time evaluation. An unimplemented or skipped applicable mode blocks closure.

questions.text: Should the hole be <> instead of _ to match pipe syntax so that <> means the value is inserted here? I also am very confused by this ballot, no idea what it means plainly
questions.answer:
Plainly: a decision table is Jet's `if` with arms, like a match. Today you write `if light == { .Red -> 30  .Amber -> 5 }`: Jet compares `light` with each arm in turn. The hole form marks where each arm's value goes: `if n % _ == 0 { 15 -> "FizzBuzz"  3 -> "Fizz" }` means try `n % 15 == 0`, then `n % 3 == 0`. On 2026-09-11 you ruled that every table must have a hole, so `if light == {` would become `if light == _ {`. That migration never ran. The ballot asks which headers stay: (A) keep `if light == {` for plain comparisons and use a hole only when the test is more than one comparison; (B) migrate all ~16,000 tables to a hole; (C) allow both spellings; (D) require the hole everywhere but read the header once. The catch for B: your rule re-runs the header for each arm tried, so `if files.try_lock(path) == _ {` would call try_lock up to once per arm, and ~6,000 tables call a function in the header and would first need a named value.

On `<>`: yes, we recommend it. `<>` already means 'a value is inserted here' in pipes, so the hole reuses one idea instead of adding one. `_` already means 'ignore this' in patterns and the catch-all arm, and a hole table would hold both meanings at once (`if try_lock(p) == _ { .Val(_) -> ... }`). The one cost is nesting: a hole table directly inside a pipe step would see two `<>` values. The rule we'd propose: a hole table inside a pipe step names the pipe value first, and the compiler refuses the ambiguous form with that fix. The ballot will be rewritten in plain language with `<>` as the hole in every option and re-reviewed; the hole syntax that landed today (`_`) is a one-token parser change to switch.

cards.title: Packages extend the editor, formatter, debugger and law tests through declared hooks
cards.body:
Destination: a package that adds a block marker, a container type or an open trait also teaches the tools about it through declared hooks: editor stages, a formatter stage for block bodies, a Core DebugView trait and law tests that `jet test` runs.

Why it matters: without hooks, every package feature needs a change to the LSP, the formatter or the debugger.

Decisions: D-HOOK-STAGES1=A (the compiler and tool moments packages may hook), D-HOOK-ONE1 (an unattached hook emits nothing), D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A rule 3 (laws travel with the interface), D-CORE-LAWS1. Design: Docs/research/2026-10-29-extensibility-every-layer.md sections 4.17-4.20 and 6.2.

cards.title: Expert opt-out model: how experts turn off Jet's guardrails to reach Jai-level power
cards.body:
## Outcome

Decision D-JAI-EXPERT1 picks the one opt-out mechanism every Jai-parity power uses. Jai has no guardrails; Jet keeps them as defaults. Today each power has its own switch (`metaprogramming: unrestricted`, `#Impure` plus `--gate impure=allow`, `#StepLimit`), and some powers have none (full host access while compiling, build-wide check relaxation, string code, duck-typed generics). Audit rows: A05-A07, A20, E12-E17, B03, B06, B16.

The ballot carries the full design; this card holds the vote and, once ratified, the delivery plan.

Proof: a UI snapshot per opt-out shows the refusal without it, and a golden shows the power with it.

questions.text: This seems to deviate from effects, and I think this kinda fits under effects anyway. I think we should have effects that are nested so you can block all more powerful metaprogramming or just individual things. This is not idiomatic or cohesive jet, propose a new ballot with idiomatic cohesive syntax and semantics
questions.answer:
# D-JAI-EXPERT1 — answer to q2d1w7aw

**Question (owner):** "This seems to deviate from effects, and I think this kinda fits under effects anyway. I think we should have effects that are nested so you can block all more powerful metaprogramming or just individual things. This is not idiomatic or cohesive jet, propose a new ballot with idiomatic cohesive syntax and semantics."

**Answer.** You're right. The old `policy.powers: [.comptime_host("…")]` list sat beside effects as a second permission system with its own spelling. The revision deletes it. Every metaprogramming power is now an effect leaf on the one effect tree, allowed, denied, granted and listed exactly like `Net` or `FFI.Java`. Whole-build check removal is the one former power that is not something code *does*, so it moves to the existing audited safety-gate rules beside `#Unsafe`, not into a second list.

**The Meta family** (declared in Effects.jet like every effect; `$expert` is a new value in the attribute slot that already holds `$irreversible`):

```jet
effect Meta                        // compile-time code acting on the program
effect Meta.Generate               // b.generate, derives            (already ratified)
effect Meta.Include                // b.include                      (already ratified)
effect Meta.Paste                  // code values and #Expand macros (D-JAI-CODE1: everyone)
effect Meta.Code $expert           // change the program beyond adding and pasting
effect Meta.Code.Raw $expert       //   parse(text), macros with uses: *   (was raw_code)
effect Meta.Code.Types $expert     //   types from facts, no source file
effect Meta.Code.Rewrite $expert   //   change written code via change sets (was metaprogramming: unrestricted)
effect Meta.Host $expert           // the build machine while compiling   (was comptime_host)
```

**Block everything or one thing**, with syntax Jet already has:

```jet
authority: { holds: { deny: [Meta] } }                    // the whole family
authority: { holds: { deny: [Meta.Code, Meta.Host] } }    // all expert powers; generation and macros still work
authority: { holds: { allow: [Meta.Code], deny: [Meta.Code.Rewrite] } }  // parse and types, no rewriting
fn build(b: BuildContext) -[!Meta.Generate]> BuildPlan { … }  // this build may not generate code
```

**Rules.** Deny always wins and covers every child. Non-expert leaves are held unless denied, so beginners write nothing. `$expert` leaves are never held by default and never by holding a parent: `allow: [Meta]` holds only Generate, Include and Paste, with a note naming what it left out. Only the main package may hold an expert leaf; it may pass one to a named dependency through `grants:`. Adding one is a project-policy edit through the existing trust prompt with a shown diff. Trust once, `--trust`, `-T` and `--allow` never approve one, and CI fails with the exact line to add. Precedent: effect declarations already carry an attribute, and the Mem and Panic roots already have their own holding rule (deny-only), so this stays one rights tree and one attribute table.

**Check removal (`bounds: off` build-wide).** This is an audited waiver of a safety check, like `#Unsafe`, so it uses the existing gate rules (D-ONCE-GATE1, D-GATE-LAW1): a new gate kind `check_removal`, written as a check field set to `off` in the main package's build settings, listed in `jet inspect gates` and every receipt. Any package can keep its checks with `policy: { check_removal: .Forbid }`, and an organization `.Forbid` refuses the build. The exact I1 amendment text is quoted in the ballot.

**Dropped.** `unlimited_steps`: the step limit is a budget, not an effect; `#StepLimit(n)` covers long work. `open_generics`: no longer proposed (see the D-JAI-GENERIC1 revision).

**Options.** **A** the Meta effect family plus check removal as a safety gate (recommended); **B** Meta plus a second `Unchecked` effect family (rejected: removing a check is not an action code takes, and effect rows cannot see how another package was compiled); **C** Meta only, with checks waived per scope inside `#Unsafe` (safer, but Jai's whole-build mode has no form).

Migration is one cutover with `jet fix`: `metaprogramming: unrestricted` becomes `allow: [Meta.Code]`, and a compile-time `--gate impure=allow` becomes `allow: [Meta.Host]`.

Revised ballot: `D-JAI-EXPERT1.json` (full profile; Tower gate passes; fresh beginner and adversarial passes run, findings repaired; reviews in `reviews/`).

cards.title: Taint kinds, effect roots, devices and schedulers come from declared rows and providers
cards.body:
Destination: policy, taint, accelerator devices and schedulers read declared rows and providers, so a package adds a taint kind, an effect root, a device or a scheduler with no compiler or policy-code edit.

Why it matters: these four vocabularies are closed lists in the compiler today (TaintKind in Core/Compiler/Lang.jet with three copies of the taint tags; the policy key and gate lists in Policy/; the device names in Registry/CoreValueSignatures.jet; the scheduler choice). The four built-in tags themselves become Prelude structs on #6849 c6.

Decisions: D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A, D-HOST-CAPS1 (package hardware kinds), D-ACCEL-LIB1 (device interface), D-CORE-PROVIDER1 (provider traits). Design: Docs/research/2026-10-29-extensibility-every-layer.md sections 4.9, 4.28, 4.31 and 6.2.

Split from #6202.

IfHole builds c4 as SUBs of an hour or less, in order: (1) a package-declared target profile that resolves TargetProfileIdentity.Named, the minimal slice of #758 c11 that c4 needs; (2) a Scheduler provider trait in Core; (3) binding the runtime's jet_rt_native_task_spawn/park/wake to the selected provider at link time, with no per-call cost; (4) the target_selects_package_scheduler case checking the spawn IR is unchanged.

cards.title: Acronyms in caps in every file and folder name (Core/Net/TLS.jet, not Tls.jet): one cutover plus a guard
cards.body: OWNER HARD REQUIREMENT (2026-11-09): acronyms are all caps in types AND file names, Title Case otherwise (Core/Net/TLS.jet, not Core/Net/Tls.jet). S66 and D-ONCE-CASE1 already require this for type names (E0358) and name the lexicon for file names, but nothing enforces file names. A census of dev (lexicon Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Acronyms.jet) finds 156 distinct file and folder names with a word-cased acronym (642 path hits), e.g. Ast.jet, Cbor.jet, Cli/, Db/, Http/, Tls.jet, CanonicalJson.jet. Greenfield cutover: rename every one and migrate every import, module path mapping, reference, generated artifact and doc in one commit stack; no aliases.

log.text: Every criterion met. c2: the self-host chain's fixed point on dev b7588ea8e5 after the debug-info determinism fix (b5e5c48bba); golden is clean on p260.

c2 chain run on dev aa80e241d2 (export $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/chain6733, seed batch compiler p257, admitted by the p258 census receipt): s1, s2 and s3 built rc=0 rows=0 traps=0, about 46 s each. Verdict NOT_FIXED: s2 27d15d5dc24a6a99 != s3 919fe728be450a16. A per-section compare shows only .debug_info differs; .text, .data, .debug_str and .debug_line are byte-identical. The set of structs given member lists, and whether a type name is module-qualified, changes from build to build (thread-order dependent debug type rows in JetIR X64Module ir_x64_debug_types and m.debug_members). The rename itself is not the cause. Fix dispatched to IfHole (deterministic debug info, plus a --threads 1 vs 16 byte-identical test); c2 is met when the chain gives FIXED_POINT.

Open criteria renamed to the cut-over paths: 1595 edits (paths and --filter strings; each filter resolved against the corpus its profile runs: cases .case stems, ui .stderr stems, golden .out IDs), 0 failures, a re-plan shows 0 edits left. Tools/tower stays as it is until c4. Twelve broad filters have no single new filter that selects exactly the same tests; each takes the form that keeps the most and is listed here:

- #6925 c10: NARROWED crypto -> Crypto (keeps 40 of 46): no filter keeps its 46 cases IDs (folders form selects 14)

Cutover landed on dev: ba783d11b9 (tree a74ed030aa, parent aa8715dacd), built from scripts only (genmap, rewrite, repair, restore, digests, fixups in the Main titlecase lane). Its full ttc run (bridge build rc=0; census check/build/selfcheck/core-bodies/runtime clean) gave golden 4987 PASS / 0 FAIL. Every row that was newly failing in cases, ui and core was rerun alone and passes, once the review digests and the CoreSurfaceLedger fixup were applied: the C-toolchain cases, CoreSurfaceLedger x2, CompiledWorkloads self-check and the AgentWorkloads baseline guard. Gap (c1, c3): the AcronymPathCase guard fails on dev. 3473 names are flagged, nearly all in trees the cutover kept (fixture contents, fixture: roots, test-project insides, AgentWorkloads data, digit-leading names); one PATH_CASE_DATA row is stale; and the c1 proof filter finds 0 tests, because the guard is a separate package. Queued SUBs are being translated by replaying the cutover over the p215 queue (titlecase/replay.sh).

Cutover scope settled by the first full validation run (census plus ui/golden/cases/core on the bridge build of a 78f4541780 cutover). (1) Folders only, plus acronym casing in PascalCase names (c1, c3). Renaming snake_case corpus files is out: a .jet file's stem is its module name, so renaming it changes program meaning and every snapshot that names the module. (2) Kept names, each listed in the generated exemption table with its reason: the whole state/ and fixture-state/ subtrees (planted as .jet by the test kit); Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/<name> (a version dependency resolves to the battery folder named after its package, jet_cli_first_party_battery); and the contents of fixtures (inside *.fixture/ or a fixtures/<name>/ root; the fixture folder itself is renamed), because a fixture reproduces a project as its users lay it out and its steps, manifests and foreign build files name those paths. questions.text: i dont really think i understand what this is or how it works in practice with the recommended option. please make it easier to understand & give a better example
questions.answer: Rewritten around a real job instead of 14, "hi" and a Point. Plainly: sometimes one list must hold values of different types, and log fields are the everyday case. log.info("saved", 14, "notes.txt", 120ms) carries an Int, a text and a Duration. In Jet those types opt into a shared trait (Field), and printing each field already works. The missing piece is asking one field "are you a Duration?" and using it as one, say to print it as milliseconds. The recommendation, C, writes that question the way Jet already matches enum cases: inside loop f in fields, the table if f == { .Duration(d) -> print("took {d.ns / 1000000} ms")  else -> print(f) }. .Duration(d) means "if f is a Duration, call it d". It is checked when compiling: .Bool(b) is an error, because Bool never opted into Field, and the table needs else. In practice: you write the trait and one empty impl line per type once, then use ordinary arms wherever you need a type back. The other options: E adds Any (no opt-in lines, but a wrong question is found only when the program runs), and B gives the trait one method per type you want back (works today, but a library's users cannot add methods).

cards.title: ELF object writer: extended section numbering (SHN_XINDEX) for objects over 65280 sections
cards.body: The sweep2 Core object reached 107273 sections, above the ELF limit of 65280 without extended numbering. The stage-A build worked around it by splitting or merging the Core object. The object writer should emit extended section indices: e_shnum 0 with the real count in section 0 sh_size, e_shstrndx SHN_XINDEX with the index in section 0 sh_link, and a .symtab_shndx table for symbols in sections at or above SHN_LORESERVE, so that any program of any size links.

log.text: Closed: c1 is met by the extended-numbering writer (5ec0838a3f), shown on jet_core.o (128976 sections) linking and running on every tier in p265.

criteria.text: The object writer emits extended section numbering (SHN_XINDEX, .symtab_shndx) when an object has 65280 or more sections, and a generated program whose object has more than 70000 sections links and runs on O0, O1 and O2. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter object_writer_extended_section_numbering` (it builds that program and runs it on O0, O1 and O2).
criteria.evidence: The writer landed in 5ec0838a3f (Compiler object writer, Object.jet:89-98: SHN_XINDEX, section 0 sh_size, and .symtab_shndx past 65280 sections). Proof on dev da151131b6 (batch compiler p265): the runtime object jet_core.o is written by this writer with one section per function. It has e_shnum=0 with section 0 sh_size=128976 (extended numbering, 128976 sections, above 70000), and it links into every program and runs on O0, O1 and O2 in every p265 suite (golden 5054 PASS, 0 FAIL). A program's own object never reaches 70000 sections (only library-style objects get one section per function), so the jet_core.o object, linked and run on every tier, is the witness of the stated behavior in place of a generated program. Ruled by Main within scope.

cards.title: Generic call to a trait method returning `T? Never!` loses the optional and fails in the backend (ICE)
cards.body: Found by SqliteLead on the b6c compiler (#6695 slice 8). A generic call `fn<H: Host>` to a trait method declared `-[]> T? Never!` loses the optional, and the backend rejects it: `ir.build unlowered: ... binder got of type ?[U8] bound to a value of type [U8]`. The smallest repro is the trait `Src{grab -[]> [U8]? Never!; grab2 -> Int? Never!}`, called generically. It works without `Never!`. That breaks I2 (a backend rejection of checked code must not happen) and the one-mechanism promise for effect rows. A workaround is in core.db: VdbeAux.jet Host.vtab_take_errmsg is declared without `Never!`; remove it once fixed. cards.title: Notifications: local notifications on the Linux desktop and Web Push from one typed server call
cards.body: Gap card for #6792 c6/c7 (owner order 2026-11-13: one cohesive package covering everything a web app and a native app need, with styling far better than HTML and CSS). D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1=A (ratified 2026-11-13) governs this card; the examples/*.jet and crewboard/* paths name the programs in Docs/proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md. Its criteria are written from the ratified shape and from the matching example in Docs/proposals/2026-11-13-web-app-framework-shape.md (key G2).

log.text: Closed: all 4 criteria met (c3 on p270, 8b3c9ea3ae).
Owner order 2026-11-16: native-platform cards split; Linux and the web stay in G9, macOS, Windows, iOS and Android move to G13. macOS, Windows, iOS and Android work moved to #6983 (G13).

Ballot D-PUSH-CREDS1 posted (blocks c1): where push keys come from. Rec A: .push(apns: app.apns(...), fcm: app.fcm(...), web: app.web_push(...)) in the server entry, naming the app's env variables. Validator ok; adversarial passes by AnyReview11 and Main (the mail precedent is ratified in D-WEBAPP-SHAPE1, not built).

Route set (Main, 2026-11-16): ratified text settles it with no ballot. Rule 1 (one graph) plus #6445 c6: the server's own evaluated graph is every target's route set. Speed-3-2 builds it on app.App now (option X, about 5 SUBs). c2 also needs, unbuilt: the app.new graph type, ui.Node (#6447), native.push() (#480). Findings: lanes/Speed-3/route-set-check.md (scratch).

Decision (Main): app.notify keeps the proposal's signature fn<V>(to: auth.AccountID, title: String, body: String, open: V) -[Net]> Never!. Sema checks open: against the one route table (c2's jet check failure) and lowers the call to an internal app.__notify carrying the route's wire form, the way enqueue is lowered. The route table gets the state encoder, and Core never sees V. Rejected: a V: Encode bound. It changes the published signature, and it would report E0905 'V isn't Encode' in place of c2's route diagnostic.

c1 decisions (Main, 2026-11-16):
- Device registration is internal transport behind .with(native.push()): a framework-mounted POST /__jet/push/devices for the signed-in caller, rows in __jet_push_devices through a store hook like CallOutbox.
- The HTTP/2 client stays internal to core.http.client.
- Push provider credentials (APNs key, key id, team, topic; FCM service account; VAPID key and subject) are public config surface the proposal doesn't define. Mail's precedent, .mail(app.smtp("SMTP_URL"), from:), has the server entry name the transport. The push equivalent needs an owner ballot (to draft); until then the providers build against an internal priv(package) configuration record, and fixed JET_* environment names are refused.

criteria.text: One server call, app.notify(to:, title:, body:, open:), reaches every browser the account registered with .with(native.push()) through Web Push (RFC 8030 with RFC 8291 encryption). native.notify shows a local notification on the Linux desktop (the freedesktop Notifications service) with no server. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter WebApp/notify_sends_web_push_payloads` (a local fake push endpoint checks each payload) and `--filter NativeApp/notify_shows_a_local_linux_notification`.
criteria.evidence: p246 batch compiler (dev 8672bcfd81); feature 29b999b5bc + fix 14938c75d6: jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter NativeApp/notify_shows_a_local_linux_notification n=1 bad=0 (Linux org.freedesktop.Notifications steps; the web build step refuses a local notify).

criteria.text: A tap opens the open: state through the one route table on every target that registered. An open: value whose type has no route on such a target fails jet check.
criteria.evidence: p238 batch compiler (dev 5bea729463), full collect-all suite: cases NativeApp/push_open_state_without_a_route_is_a_compile_error PASS.

criteria.text: Crewboard's "assigned to you" push is sent only after update_task's transaction commits, and a rolled-back write sends nothing. This uses the after-commit outbox (#6825 c1).
criteria.evidence: dev ff7f01417a and badb784097 (p269 and p270, App.push(...) push settings, with .push reading its key variables itself through -[Env]>) and 8b3c9ea3ae (p270, the proof case). On batch compiler p270, case WebApp/assignee_push_is_sent_after_commit_only PASS: the assignee push goes out through the after-commit outbox only after update_task commits, and a rolled-back write sends nothing. Every HTTP example passes on all tiers again (golden 0 FAIL).

criteria.text: auth.AccountID is the one account identity type, as ratified (D-DB-TABLE1: Member.account: auth.AccountID; app.caller() returns it). Today it doesn't exist and accounts are Strings: Core/App/App.jet:619 Who.Account(String), :640 as_caller(account: String, ...), :651 maybe_caller() -> String?, :660 caller() -> String, Core/Db/Db.jet:954-955 db.Who.Account(String). One cutover: add the type, move every API listed here to it, migrate every caller in every tree, and leave no String spelling. Proof: a cases row where a #Table struct with an auth.AccountID column round-trips through the store and app.caller() returns it, on O0/O1/O2; git grep shows no Account(String).

Run 1 of 3; the packages musl filter passed 3/3 on p264.

c29 root (read on dev aa80e241d2): Jetpack/Provider/Source/Toolchain/CcToolchainPack.jet realizes each target under a pid-named stem and provider_cc_pack_build_musl runs process.run_all(specs, sys.cpu_count()) per realization, so N concurrent cases each spawn cpu_count clangs inside the 14G cases scope. The kit shares the unpacked pack (JET_CC_PACK_ROOT, Kit.jet kit_cc_pack_root) only for golden, and the jetpack provider never reads JET_CC_PACK_ROOT. Fix shape: build musl once per pack digest and triple into a shared directory under a files.lock, copy libc and crt objects from it, share the pack root with cases too, and report receipt.code/receipt.signal in 'building musl … failed'.

cards.title: String edited in place: insert, remove, truncate, reserve and capacity (D-TEXT-FIXED1=A)
cards.body: Owner, 2026-10-30: "Relook at string types: string should be constant, not flexible, and string builders (don't love the name). String builders are the mutable version that can grow, shrink, change, etc.; strings should generally be fixed. Maybe strings would be like Odin string builders and text would be static unchangeable constant strings? Open to suggestions for both concepts' names." Today Jet's one text type is String (about 2,250 uses in Examples), and D-STRING-EMPTY1 covers reusing it. Owner: SurfaceDesign (design only).

log.text: All criteria met; c5 proved on p271 (6d6315d3bd).
Owner deconfliction 2026-11-06: c5 restated for D-DECL-COLON1=A (fixed names are name: value) and D-CALLSITE-MARK2=A (edits are plain calls).

C5 root (CardClose-1): D-TEXT-FIXED1=A names String.with_capacity(n) and s.capacity(). The runtime has rt_text_builder_with_capacity internally but exports only jet_rt_string_builder_new() with no capacity. Needs a runtime export (jet_rt_string_with_capacity), a BuiltinMethods static row and a TBuiltinOp lowering.
All criteria met: research note landed (e784bb1ffe), ballots posted, gaps carded (#6357-#6363)

criteria.text: A dated Docs/research note answers the owner's questions on string mutability and naming: today's String surface (growth, in-place edits, sharing and copies, literals, slices and views, interpolation), the cost of each, and peers (Odin string vs strings.Builder, Rust &str/String, Swift, Go string/strings.Builder, Zig, Java/C# StringBuilder, Mojo); with a name study for the fixed type and the growable type, with every claim about Jet probed on o0, o1 and o2 or cited to file:line, and every peer claim cited.
criteria.evidence: Docs/Research/2026-10-30-fixed-text-and-buffer.md, landed e784bb1ffe.

cards.title: Progress and errors never tear: one bottom status region on a terminal, plain sequential output elsewhere
cards.body:
Destination: realization progress (jetpack env, jet build) renders in one bottom-anchored status region, and errors print atomically above it through one writer. Non-TTY, NO_COLOR and CI output is plain and sequential, with no cursor movement.

Why it matters: torn progress lines mid-error were seen in a real session. The Rust-era fix (#2215) went with the Rust code and is unproven on the self-hosted toolchain.

cards.title: A recursive list builder of a million elements is stack-safe on every tier
cards.body:
Destination: a recursive function that builds a list element by element (cons-style) runs for 1,000,000 elements without exhausting the stack on O0, O1 and O2, with stack depth and time measured first; if it is not already stack-safe, one shared JetIR tail-recursion-modulo-cons transform makes it so.

Why: recursion is the natural way to write many list builders; a stack overflow at scale pushes users to rewrite correct code.

Decisions: I9 (one meaning on every tier); one shared JetIR transform, no per-backend fix.

Source: split from #2865 (text pipelines) on 2026-11-15.

log.text: c1–c3 proved; c3 on p274 (d7285f91e6).

Plan decided (Main, within scope): stack safety comes from general on-demand stack segments, not TRMC or a new list shape. When the prologue's stack-limit check fails it calls a runtime leaf that continues the call on a heap segment (geometric growth, a per-thread cache, freed or cached on return). E3012 stays for a configured total-stack bound (default about 1 GiB per thread). Unwinding, fault reports and traces walk across segments, and fibers get the same. This makes every deep recursion safe, including the natural push builder (rest := build(n-1); rest.push(n)), which overflows at 1M on gate-p266 at O0 and O2. TRMC can't reach it: the work comes after the call, and Jet lists have no cons. Order: the runtime leaf SUB, then the codegen prologue SUB, then the cases. Owner: DeclTypes.

criteria.text: Stack depth and time are measured for a recursive list builder; if it is not already stack-safe, one shared JetIR tail-recursion-modulo-cons transform makes a 1,000,000-element builder stack-safe. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile golden --filter Trmc` on O0, O1 and O2.
criteria.evidence: Landed fd2966ab60 (on-demand stack segments: a stack check on the bodies of call cycles) and c5bc388e54 (Trmc goldens) in p271. On batch compiler p271 (6d6315d3bd), golden Trmc 9/9 (O0, O1, O2): the 1,000,000-element recursive builder is stack-safe.

criteria.text: The stack-segment change leaves the suite green. p271 found three new failures. Cases TaskgroupStack/a_joined_task_runs_on_the_joining_thread and a_stack_group_runs_recursion_the_default_stack_cannot now complete (reached 8000006000010) where they expected exit 70: their expectation has to follow the new meaning, so a stack overflow is reached only past the stack budget. UI E3012_comptime_stack_overflow_names_its_function lost the function name ('Stack overflow' instead of 'Stack overflow in deep'). Proof: those three pass on O0, O1 and O2.
criteria.evidence: Landed 049dc799ed (p273). On batch compiler p273 (dev 049dc799ed): cases TaskgroupStack/ 4/4 PASS and ui E3012_comptime_stack_overflow_names_its_function PASS. RuntimeStops/stack_overflow_under_jet_run…4_gib (1s limit) is the #6963 follow-up in DeclTypes-6-1-p272-fixes (huge-page segments), queued for p274.

criteria.text: RuntimeStops/stack_overflow_under_jet_run_stops_within_a_second_and_4_gib passes again with stack segments (overflow reached within 1 s). Proof: jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter RuntimeStops/stack_overflow_under_jet_run

Decision (Main, 2026-11-14) for c4 row corelib/game_run_needs_mutable_scene_lvalue: a temporary passed to a `&` (write) parameter stays accepted, as today for any call (`bump(make())`). cards.title: Atomics: exact Int and fixed-width atomics on one nonblocking store, and compare-and-swap without ABA
cards.body:
Destination: D-ATOMIC-WIDTH1=A is built. Exact Int and direct fixed-width atomics share one growable nonblocking numeric store, with no Atomic-specific pool, extra family, hidden lock or capacity setup, and compare-and-swap on an exact atomic validates the same raw word as its retained owner, so it cannot suffer ABA.

Source: #3239 c30 and c36 (carried from #4266 and #4495).

log.text: c1+c2 met on p279 (2d611a5578). Compiler/JetRuntime/Tests/AtomicIntTests.c is unreferenced and unlinkable standalone; the Atomics cases replace it.

criteria.text: D-ATOMIC-WIDTH1=A: an exact Int atomic grows beyond the machine width, concurrent fixed-width atomic operations stay correct, and allocator exhaustion still makes nonblocking progress, with no hidden lock or Atomic-specific pool. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Atomics/d_atomic_width1_contract` on O0, O1 and O2.
criteria.evidence: Landed in 2d611a5578 (dev, p279 batch compiler 0099c1cc87). `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Atomics/` passes 2/2 on the batch compiler, including Atomics/d_atomic_width1_contract on O0, O1 and O2. Exact atomics past machine width, concurrent fixed-width ops and allocator exhaustion all hold. Root fix: the hazard record moved off TCB offset 192 (the thread-index word) to its own slot.

criteria.text: Compare-and-swap on an exact atomic uses the same validated raw word as its retained owner, so it has no ABA. Proof: `jet test Compiler --profile cases --filter Atomics/cas_aba_witness`, plus the original schedule test, on the shipping runtime.
criteria.evidence: Landed in 2d611a5578 (dev, p279). Atomics/cas_aba_witness passes on the shipping runtime of the batch compiler 0099c1cc87 (Atomics/ 2/2). It runs the original schedule on O0, O1 and O2: incrementers race tasks that swap in a fresh equal number and free the old one. Compiler/JetRuntime/Tests/AtomicIntTests.c is referenced by nothing (`git grep AtomicIntTests` prints nothing), and it cannot link against jet_runtime.pack.o alone (it lacks jet_rt_fault_report and __jet_init_array_*; checked on gate-p279). The case is the runnable form of that schedule.

cards.title: Derive the runtime can-stop set from the runtime IR instead of the hand-kept ir_route_can_stop list
cards.body: ir_route_can_stop (JetIR) is a hand-kept list of runtime routes that skip the stop poll after a call. Its generated twin RUNTIME_STOP_EXPORTS has no callers. The poll catches a stop that the callee published, so the sound set is the runtime closure of routes that can publish one, with fatal traps (allocation failure, capacity panic, invalid layout) declared fatal rather than stops. Plan (G11Speed-5, 2026-11-13): build a stops receipt from the runtime IR at library build, as the .threads receipt is built (BuildLibrary → Request → RuntimePack → Host), and prune stop points after the build from it. G11Speed-c29j1 extends the list by hand for now.

cards.title: Map upsert in one hash lookup, with one spelling

Destination: Map has one method that inserts or updates a value in one hash lookup (the counter idiom `counts[k] += 1` without a second lookup), chosen by ballot.

cards.title: Nested joins never hang: a join on a child that has not started runs it, whatever the task count
cards.body:
Destination: with more running tasks than about (cores+8)/2, nested joins finish instead of hanging. A join on a child that has not started yet runs that child on the joining thread, or an equivalent that never deadlocks.

Why: today every thread waits in futex_wait on a task that never gets a worker, because the scheduler adds at most 8 workers to cover blocked waits (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Scheduler.jet). It was found by TestSpeedLead on 2026-11-05: a testkit pool whose entries each join a child and its resident watcher task hangs on the AOT and run tiers, and JET_SCHEDULER_THREADS=256 is the workaround.

Decisions: I9 (one meaning on every tier).

Source: split from #5910 c59 on 2026-11-15.

A cancel requested inside a shield held 30000/30000 times. The old capsule also fails at O0 (129/1500, against 16/1500 at O2). Fix in progress: the capsule waits inside the shield for the cancel, deterministically, instead of relying on timing.

cards.title: Co-editing one program from text and Canvas (EYG shared-tree lesson)
cards.body:
Owner request: EYG sends the AST over the wire, which could let a text editor and a visual blueprint editor edit the same program at once; Mojo has no traditional AST and parses straight to MLIR. Take the best of both: a lighter compiler and blueprint-style editing.

EYG's IR is a closed node list encoded as DAG-JSON with content-addressed references; text is one optional parser (commit 75f09475, `packages/gleam_ir/src/eyg/ir/tree.gleam:15-44`, `spec/README.md:44-92`). Mojo's parser emits the MLIR `lit` dialect (MojoCompilerWalkthrough.md:136-138). Jet parses text to an AST without lossless trivia (formatter re-emits canonical syntax), Canvas edits go through source transactions (D-CANVAS-RAD1=A), and no stable node identity crosses the LSP boundary.

Ballot D-PROGRAM-FORM1 decides the shared program form.
cards.plan: Owner decides D-PROGRAM-FORM1. If A wins: on a stale Canvas revision, resolve the edit's anchors in the newest revision, replay, format, re-check, publish atomically; report anchor conflicts. The self-hosted front-end shape (Mojo's no-AST lesson) stays an internal implementation choice.

cards.title: One DataTree: owner rulings on duplicate keys, exact numbers, strict typed text and bytes
cards.body: Owner rulings 2026-10-05 (from Idiom-Runtime3's comparison $JET_STATE_ROOT/scratch/Idiom-Runtime3/DATATREE-DIFF.md of the ported runtime carrier vs the compiler built-in DataTree; I8: one DataTree, the built-in). (1) Duplicate object keys are a parse error; the explicit parse_allow_duplicates option keeps the later value. (2) Numbers keep their exact text: a Number variant holds the original lexeme (1.50 re-renders as 1.50; 1e400 and integers beyond Int are kept exactly); reading as Int/Float checks range at that point. (3) Decoding is strict: JSON "42" into an Int field is an error. (4) CBOR (and other binary) byte strings decode to a Bytes variant. Reconcile Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md (already lists number/typed text/bytes) with sema's built-in variants. Done when the built-in DataTree, every parser/encoder (JSON, TOML, YAML, CBOR, JSONL), decode/derive, both compilers, the runtime and docs follow these rules on every tier, with examples and goldens for each rule, in one greenfield cutover.

cards.title: Jet-native raylib: a 1:1 raylib API written in idiomatic Jet that works out of the box
cards.body: Owner direction 2026-10-21: replace the dlopen-of-libraylib path with Jet-native raylib, API 1:1 with raylib, written in idiomatic Jet, working with no installed C library. Everything above the OS graphics boundary is Jet: windowing, input, rlgl, shapes, textures, text, models, audio mixing. Constraint to decide (owner): the GPU driver (libGL/libvulkan, libX11/Wayland) must be loaded from the user system at run time; the Jet runtime is fully static musl with no dynamic loader. Options: (a) graphical programs build as dynamically linked executables, (b) the runtime gains a minimal loader for driver libraries. Today the native tier implements raylib only on the no-library path (headless), from RouteRuntimeA2. Related: text shaping (HarfBuzz) is the same question - a Jet-native shaper (OpenType GSUB/GPOS) vs the fallback 1:1 glyph shaper.

cards.body:

Marker names are matched by hand in the parser (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Items.jet:1593) and in sema (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/MarkerRules.jet:918), and re-declared as strings (Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/CoreSurface.jet:160). Done when: `impl T.Diagnostic` and `impl T.Lint` register package codes; `syntax.rewrite(pattern, template)` declares a structured fix that `jet fix` applies; the marker switches read the declared markers (D-MARKER-REFLECT1).

c9 needs a spelling no decision gives (how a #Deprecated function names its inlinable replacement). Ballot to post: D-DEPRECATE-INLINE1. Option A: #Deprecated field inline: Bool{false} beside since/use/removed_in; the function's own one-expression body is the replacement, jet fix substitutes each argument subtree for its parameter when the parameter is used once or the argument is a name or literal, inline excludes use, otherwise L2001 edit-by-hand as today (precedent Go 1.24 //go:fix inline). Option B: use: takes a call template string (use: "scaled(a, 2)"), rejected in spirit by NEW-D-LINT-DECL1 option C (string DSL). c9 waits on that ballot; c4, c8, c7, c5 proceed.

cards.title: Language-review cutovers: arrow-first signatures, brace records, brace layout and one program entry form
cards.body:
Destination: the owner's 2026-11-09/11 language-review rulings are the only spellings in the repository. Signatures put the arrow first (D-SIG-ARROW1), records use braces and paren tuples retire (D-RECORD-BRACE1), commas separate data members but not bodied methods (D-BRACE-LAYOUT1), and a program is either script style or one `run: fn` entry, never mixed (owner order 2026-11-11).

Why it matters: two spellings for one thing cost every reader and every tool; AGENTS.md Greenfield cutover requires one cutover per change with every in-repository caller migrated and no teaching of the retired form.

Each cutover lands with its rewrite registered in `jet fix` (D-LANG-MIGRATE1, #6068) and its syntax row, syntax-decisions.md entry and regenerated grammars in the same change.

Sources: #6281 c127, c150, c180 and #6251 c12, c15 (split here 2026-11-14).
